final_proof:
For each a in {1,...,m}, put S_a={i∈I:x_a(i)≠0}. By the definition of A, every S_a is countable. Hence J=⋃_{a=1}^m S_a is countable, being a finite union of countable sets. Choose an injection e:J→ℕ₀.

We first record the relation between generalized sums and series that will be used below. If (c_i)_{i∈I} is a family of nonnegative real numbers which vanishes outside J, its generalized sum is the limit of the net

    s_F=∑_{i∈F}c_i

over the finite subsets F of I, ordered by inclusion. This net is increasing. Consequently, whenever it converges, its limit is

    sup{∑_{i∈F}c_i:F⊂I finite}
     =sup{∑_{i∈F}c_i:F⊂J finite}.                 (1)

Define a sequence (z_n) by z_{e(i)}=c_i for i∈J and z_n=0 for n∉e(J). For every N,

    ∑_{n=0}^N z_n=∑_{i∈J, e(i)≤N}c_i.             (2)

The set on the right is finite. Conversely, every finite subset F of J is contained in {i∈J:e(i)≤N} for some N (with the empty set causing no difficulty). It follows from (1) and (2) that, whenever the generalized sum exists,

    ∑_{n=0}^∞ z_n=∑_{i∈I}c_i.                     (3)

The same conclusion holds if one merely knows that the finite subsums of (c_i) are bounded: both sides then exist, by monotone completeness of the real numbers, and equal their common supremum.

For each a∈{1,...,m}, define y_a=(y_{a,n})_{n≥0} by

    y_{a,n}=x_a(i)  if n=e(i) for some i∈J,
    y_{a,n}=0       if n∉e(J).

There is at most one such i because e is injective. Apply (3) to c_i=x_a(i)^2. The generalized sum on the right converges because x_a∈A, and therefore

    ∑_{n=0}^∞ y_{a,n}^2=∑_{i∈I}x_a(i)^2<∞.        (4)

Thus y_a∈ℓ².

Fix a,b∈{1,...,m}. To justify the corresponding sum of squared differences directly, let T_a=∑_{i∈I}x_a(i)^2 and T_b=∑_{i∈I}x_b(i)^2. For every finite F⊂I,

    ∑_{i∈F}(x_a(i)-x_b(i))²
    ≤2∑_{i∈F}x_a(i)²+2∑_{i∈F}x_b(i)²
    ≤2T_a+2T_b.

Thus these nonnegative finite subsums are bounded, so their generalized sum exists. The family (x_a(i)-x_b(i))² vanishes outside J. Applying the bounded-subsums form of (3), and using the definition of the y_a, gives

    ∑_{n=0}^∞(y_{a,n}-y_{b,n})²
    =∑_{i∈I}(x_a(i)-x_b(i))².                    (5)

Both sides are nonnegative and finite. Taking nonnegative square roots in (5) yields

    d_{ℓ²}(y_a,y_b)=d₂(x_a,x_b).

It remains to verify the stated equivalence of equality, rather than deriving it implicitly from the distance formula. If x_a=x_b, their definitions immediately give y_a=y_b. Conversely, suppose y_a=y_b. For i∈J, comparison at coordinate e(i) gives x_a(i)=y_{a,e(i)}=y_{b,e(i)}=x_b(i). For i∉J, both x_a(i) and x_b(i) are zero by the definition of J. Hence x_a=x_b. Therefore y_a≠y_b if and only if x_a≠x_b, and (5) proves all the required distance equalities.
